transcript.text: Is it normal that I can hear water running in my washer dryer the whole time it's DRYING? Worried it's leaking or costing me a fortune on the water meter.

Yes, that's very likely normal. Most washer-dryers are condenser types: instead of venting steam outside, they run a steady trickle of cold water over a condenser inside the machine for the whole dry. The moisture from your clothes condenses into that water and the pump sends it down the drain hose. So hearing water trickling or running throughout drying is exactly what you'd expect. A few newer models condense with air instead and use little or no water, but water-cooled ones are still very common. On the water meter: it's usually modest. Depending on the model and programme it's often somewhere in the region of 10 to 20-odd litres per drying cycle, sometimes more on long dries. On typical UK metered rates that's usually just pennies a cycle (often under 10p). The electricity for drying normally costs far more than the water. Your manual or the energy label will give the exact figure. 1. Water on the floor. Put a dry towel along the front and sides during a drying run. If it stays dry, nothing is leaking. If it gets wet, the condensed water may be backing up. A fluff-clogged pump filter at the bottom front, or a kinked drain hose or blocked standpipe, are the usual culprits.
2. Water building up in the drum. Look through the door glass while it dries. A visible pool of water in the drum, or clothes coming out wetter than when drying started, would point to water coming in faster than it should.
3. Note the meter reading at night with the machine switched off and nothing else running, then check it again in the morning. If the floor stays dry, the drum isn't filling and it dries your clothes properly, you can relax: it's working as designed. Is the floor dry and the drum clear of water when you check during drying?

Yes, the floor is dry - I checked with kitchen roll and there's no water under or around it. Clothes come out dry as normal. I can hear the pump kick in every few minutes too. I'm not going out to read the meter though, it's in the pavement.

That all points to normal behaviour. A dry floor, clothes coming out dry, and the pump kicking in every few minutes is exactly what a water-cooled condenser washer-dryer does. The trickle you hear is cooling the condenser, and the pump is sending that water, plus the moisture taken out of your clothes, down the drain. Nothing is leaking, and the water cost per dry is small. No need to go out to the meter in the pavement. One tip to keep it that way: drying sends a lot of fluff through the pump, so clean the pump filter at the bottom front every month or two. Unplug the machine first, put a towel and a shallow tray down, and unscrew the filter slowly. That stops the condensed water backing up, and it keeps drying times short. It would be worth looking again if you ever see water on the floor, a pool building up in the drum during drying, or clothes coming out damp when they used to dry fine. Is there anything else I can help with?

Water leaking externally during drying (e.g. condensed water backing up through a blocked pump filter or drain hose) (low)
Inlet valve letting in more water than it should (water level rising in the drum) (low)

plan: They asked: "Is it normal to hear water running the whole time it's drying?" - answer that first.
The fault they reported is: "sound of water running during drying". Keep to it: never describe a symptom, result or state they have not told you.

Stage 1 (broad help): say what could cause this, most likely first, as possibilities rather than certainties, including simple causes (settings, loading, detergent, installation, or normal behaviour) where they fit. Then give the safe checks that best tell those causes apart (most useful and simplest first, usually two to four), each with why it helps and what each result would mean; or, if one question would settle it sooner, ask that. Do not ask for the model number in this reply. Do not tell them to buy, order or replace a part yet.
